name: Kuki-Chin
region: Mizoram and Manipur in northeast India, the Chin Hills of Myanmar, and the Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh
defining_innovation: Mizo, the Chin languages and Thadou, spoken across the India–Myanmar border hills, many of them written in Latin script since missionary times.

chapters.title: The Border Hills
chapters.body: The Kuki-Chin languages are spoken across the hills where India, Myanmar and Bangladesh meet. They have many languages and dialects, some spoken by only a few villages. From the 1890s Welsh and other missionaries brought Christianity and literacy, and Mizoram and the Chin Hills are now among the most Christian regions of Asia.

chapters.title: Mizo
chapters.body: In 1894 the missionaries J. H. Lorrain and F. W. Savidge devised a Latin alphabet for Mizo (then called Lushai), and literacy spread fast. Mizoram now has one of the highest literacy rates in India. When Mizoram became a Union Territory in 1972 and a state in 1987, Mizo became its official language, the language of a flourishing press and literature.

speakers.note: Rough figure: many Kuki-Chin varieties are counted inconsistently across census categories; Mizo has about 0.8 million speakers in India.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Census of India 2011. Language: India, States and Union Territories (Paper 1 of 2018). New Delhi: Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner.

turning_points.title: Into the border hills
turning_points.description: Kuki-Chin speakers spread through the hills between the Chindwin valley and the Bengal plains and diverge into many languages. How Kuki-Chin relates to the Naga languages and to Meitei is disputed.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Randy J. LaPolla, eds. 2017. The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: The Mizo alphabet
turning_points.description: Lorrain and Savidge create a Latin alphabet for Mizo, and the grammar and dictionary they publish in 1898 lay the foundation for Mizo literacy and literature.

sources.citation: Lorrain, J. Herbert & F. W. Savidge. 1898. A Grammar and Dictionary of the Lushai Language. Shillong: Assam Secretariat Printing Office.

turning_points.title: Official language of Mizoram
turning_points.description: After decades of insurgency and the 1986 peace accord, Mizoram becomes a state of India in 1987 with Mizo as its official language.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Randy J. LaPolla, eds. 2017. The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.
